entries.paper_title: Data-driven identification of predictive risk biomarkers for subgroups of osteoarthritis using interpretable machine learning
entries.prediction_task: 5-year osteoarthritis risk prediction

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Models incorporate data gathered over the subsequent five years (or until OA diagnosis), effectively conditioning on future observations. One cannot anticipate factors like NSAID use four years into the future. The study essentially assumes the form of a retrospective study, not a prediction model.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have revised the paper to clarify this is a retrospective characterization study, not a prospective prediction model. The study design section has been rewritten.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: NSAIDs are commonly prescribed for OA management and should preferably not be incorporated into a model designed to predict the onset of OA. NSAID prescriptions up to one year before OA diagnosis as a feature is essentially a proxy for existing disease.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We acknowledge this concern and have added discussion about NSAID as a potential indicator of early-stage disease rather than a predictor.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Prior studies based on UK Biobank have demonstrated that models solely incorporating age, sex, and BMI can predict OA with AUC of 0.685-0.701. It is essential to compare the authors' models with simpler models incorporating established risk factors.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added comparison with a baseline model using age, sex, and BMI only.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Inclusion of highly correlated variables (e.g., fat mass ratios in right leg vs left leg, grip strength right vs left hand) should be reconsidered to avoid multicollinearity issues.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added VIF analysis and discussed multicollinearity. Highly correlated variables were noted but retained as SHAP handles this.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Why were controls not age and sex matched, as these are fixed risk factors for OA? What exclusion criteria were applied to controls? Many EHR codes for OA are common and non-specific — discuss the role of contamination of OA subjects in the control group.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added age and sex matching analysis and discussed potential contamination. Sensitivity analysis was performed excluding borderline cases.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Although they validate their model in a separate sample in UKB, really this needs to be done in a separate cohort. This should be acknowledged.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have acknowledged this limitation in the discussion. The lack of external validation in a non-UKB cohort is noted as a key limitation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Present the ClinGRS, ClinMet and ClinPro OA risk models using SHAP values similar to how the Clin model was presented in Figure 2D. The sparse volcano plots are not particularly informative.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added SHAP summary plots for all model variants.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A major missed opportunity: the multi-omics data was not used to disentangle the role of BMI in OA. High BMI is an established predictor but the underlying reasons BMI influences OA etiology are likely diverse. The multi-omics data has potential to identify subgroups of high risk patients.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added a dedicated BMI sub-analysis using multi-omics SHAP values to examine whether different molecular pathways explain the BMI-OA association in different patient subgroups.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors should exercise caution in their claims of causality, as biomarkers may reflect processes already in motion and may not necessarily indicate a causal relationship.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have toned down causal language throughout and explicitly state that associations are observational.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: OA is a heterogeneous condition yet the majority of study participants have an undifferentiated diagnosis. There are considerable differences between joints (e.g., BMI is a bigger risk factor for knee than hip OA). Grouping all OA diagnoses introduces noise.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added joint-specific sub-analyses and acknowledged the heterogeneity limitation in the discussion.

reviewer_strengths.text: Employing interpretable machine learning techniques, the researchers successfully mapped a wide range of OA risk biomarkers. The model's robustness in accurately predicting 70% of OA cases is noteworthy.
The cross-validation approach, well-constructed matched controls, and breadth of variables included are strengths. Very good use of UK Biobank which is almost unique in its size.

entries.paper_title: Artificial intelligence in sepsis early prediction and diagnosis using unstructured data in healthcare
entries.prediction_task: Sepsis early prediction (6-48h before onset)

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The dataset is highly imbalanced; thus, AUC should not be the only performance metric reported. Authors should at least provide PPV and NPV. Furthermore, it is unclear how well calibrated the model is; calibration curves should be provided.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added PPV, NPV, sensitivity, specificity for all time horizons. Calibration curves have been added as supplementary figures.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Based on the title 'role of unstructured data', I would have expected the authors to describe the actual role of clinical notes in prediction performance, in comparison to using structured data only. The results pertain only to processing both types of data together.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added ablation study comparing: structured-only vs. notes-only vs. combined, showing the incremental value of unstructured data.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The method of labelling sepsis prediction is unusual and a potential source of significant confusion: 'when a physician orders for both culture test and lactate test, we classify the patient as one predicted to have sepsis by the physician.' The authors do not provide any evidence to the validity of this crucial statement.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added clinical validation of this labeling approach with references to Rhee et al. 2017 and Singer et al. 2016 Sepsis-3 criteria, and sensitivity analysis with alternative labeling.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: When developing the model, cross-validation is much more robust method to avoid overfitting than the random split used by the authors.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added 5-fold cross-validation results alongside the holdout results, showing consistent performance.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: How was random sampling performed? Was the unit of randomization performed at the level of the note, the patient visit, or the patient? Was there any overlap in patients between the test set and the training/validation set?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Splitting was performed at the patient level. No patient appears in both training and test sets. This has been clarified in the methods.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The paper is missing a demographics table to describe the patient population. What is the incidence of sepsis, severe sepsis, septic shock? How many are admitted to the ICU? Age distribution?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Table 1 has been added with full demographic and clinical characteristics of the cohort.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It would be helpful to include a reliability diagram (calibration diagram) as well as a precision-recall diagram for a representative model to better understand calibration and trade-offs between precision and recall for choosing a decision threshold.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Calibration plots and precision-recall curves have been added as supplementary figures.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A standard CONSORT enrollment diagram should be included as a figure to show patient flow.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Flow diagram has been added as Figure 1.

reviewer_strengths.text: The background is well motivated. Using ML for real-time surveillance and workflow augmentation for decreasing variability in care is eloquently stated.
Performance characteristics persist even 12 hours prior to sepsis onset (AUC 0.94), which is considerably better than comparison papers.

entries.paper_title: Development of a long noncoding RNA-based machine learning model to predict COVID-19 in-hospital mortality
entries.prediction_task: COVID-19 in-hospital mortality prediction

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The demographics are missing ethnic data which research has shown drastically affect risk assessing algorithms. Key data such as prior medical history, or ongoing treatment for other conditions is important to address or at least mention in limitations.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added demographic and clinical characteristics in Table 1 (diabetes, chronic lung disease, cardiovascular disease, oxygen therapy). Ethnicity was available only in NAPKON cohort. Limitations section updated.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Missing data was imputed without specifying its percentage. For example, was 40% of the age variable missing in cohort A? These characteristics need to be mentioned for assessment of the lncRNA as a potential biomarker.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Missing data percentages have been added to Table 1. In the discovery cohort, 0.5% age, 18.7% smoking were missing. No missing gene expression data.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Was the input data imputed for the validation cohort? If yes, then what were missing proportions? These parameters could skew the results in favor of the biomarker.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Age was the only clinical variable selected for ML from the validation cohort. Since all patients had age information, there was no imputation needed. Results are not skewed.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors do not include reference to the TRIPOD guidelines, which are the gold-standard for reporting risk stratification models.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added TRIPOD checklist compliance as supplementary material.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: AUC says little about performance across the range of risk and interpretation in isolation should be avoided. How do they compare not only in AUC value but in assessing calibration and possible 'real-world' performance through DCA analysis?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added calibration curves and DCA analysis comparing our model with existing COVID-19 mortality prediction models.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A number of high-quality risk stratification models for predicting inpatient mortality for COVID-19 already exist (see Wynants et al living review in BMJ). What is their comparative performance compared to the novel model described?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added systematic comparison with published COVID-19 mortality models from the Wynants et al. living review.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Another way to further tease apart the relative importance of lncRNA expression would be to show a Shapley beeswarm plot of the feature weights for the models. Ideally we could see this for one of the larger models with additional lncRNAs.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: SHAP beeswarm plots have been added for the expanded model with additional lncRNAs.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It might be possible to improve the model performance using a gradient-boosted tree model. Since this is a very simple code change, it would be worthwhile to see if XGBoost might allow the model to glean additional information from other lncRNAs.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We tested XGBoost and gradient boosting classifiers. Results showed marginal improvement. Added to supplementary comparison table.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I did not find the file with code.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Code has been uploaded to GitHub and the repository link has been added to the Data Availability section.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I may have missed something, but I didn't see a link to the code.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Code repository link added.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I would like to better understand the extent to which LEF1-AS1 expression is independent of age and gender, which are both known risk factors. How correlated is LEF1-AS1 expression with these demographic variables?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: LEF1-AS1 was weakly and negatively correlated to age (r=-0.21 discovery, r=-0.35 validation). Added correlation plot as Figure 2D.

reviewer_strengths.text: The scale of the cohorts is significantly larger than previous work, so the conclusions are more likely to be robust. The classifier performs relatively well, suggesting possible clinical utility.
This is an interesting study with exciting results of translational value.

entries.paper_title: TransformEHR: transformer-based encoder-decoder generative model to enhance prediction of disease outcomes using electronic health records
entries.prediction_task: Disease outcome prediction from longitudinal EHR (pancreatic cancer onset, self-harm in PTSD)

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: AUROC reported only for Pancreatic Cancer in the main manuscript. Supplement tables show Jaccard scores, which is inappropriate for discriminative accuracy. Move main results to main manuscript and report AUROC, AUPRC, and other metrics with best-defined thresholds.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We replaced Jaccard with AUROC as primary metric and added comprehensive metrics to the main manuscript.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: PPV 1.7% - is this really practically useful? If implemented in clinical practice, over 98% of interventions would be for patients who will not actually harm themselves. The statement that PPV 8.45% 'minimizes resource cost' is certainly not true as stated.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have revised the language to more accurately describe the clinical trade-offs. Added cost-effectiveness analysis using ICER thresholds.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Please clarify the meaning of what you are predicting. ICD-10-CM is how the meaning is encoded but does not fully explain what is being predicted. Are these codes entered for billing purposes? Clinical purposes? Without this, it is hard to understand the contribution beyond numerical comparison.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We clarified that ICD-10-CM codes reflect clinical diagnoses documented during VA encounters, and added discussion of billing vs clinical coding practices.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The VA and MIMIC populations are clinically very different (general vs ICU). It is surprising that a system pretrained on a general population performed well on a very different population. More information regarding prediction tasks in different populations needed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added detailed analysis of domain shift between VA and MIMIC populations and discussed transfer learning properties.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Prediction of pancreatic cancer ICD-10 codes one visit prior may not be clinically useful. The documentation of a code is not equivalent to the first diagnosis. The duration between visits may differ greatly — predicting in 1 year may be much more useful than if next visit is in 1 week.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added a new prediction window (12-36 months) for pancreatic cancer onset and updated results for this clinically meaningful timeframe.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The use of PHI data like actual visit dates will highly impact both usability and generalizability. Recommend using day differences between events instead.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We implemented daysdiff embedding and showed no significant performance difference vs date-specific embedding, while improving privacy protection.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The improvements in PPV over BERT are relatively modest in absolute terms (7.14% vs 8.67%). Is this clinically significant? How much does this practically decrease resource utilization?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added cost-effectiveness analysis showing ICER reduction from baseline, demonstrating practical clinical significance.

reviewer_strengths.text: Methods are well-described and appropriate, with ablation analyses to help determine the most useful model components as well as analyzing model performance in different patient subgroups based on demographics.

entries.paper_title: Biology-guided deep learning predicts prognosis and cancer immunotherapy response
entries.prediction_task: Gastric cancer prognosis and immunotherapy response prediction from CT images

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A lot more detail needs to be provided on which parts of the CT images were used and correlated to histology images. Which cut of CT was used and why? Were they sagittal or cross-sectional? It is almost impossible to visualize a stomach tumor on CT, especially early stages. It is non-trivial to correlate a biopsy from endoscopy and match to a CT scan.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added detailed description of CT slice selection, tumor segmentation protocol, and histology-radiology correlation methods.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Given that stage is a very good determinant of prognosis, how do we know that the ML model isn't merely measuring tumor size and using this to determine prognosis? What other features other than size is the model using? How do we know it isn't merely using clinicopathological characteristics already readily available?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added ablation analysis removing size-related features and showed the model captures additional information beyond tumor size. Multivariate analysis demonstrates DLS is independent of stage.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: For prediction of benefit for adjuvant chemotherapy, a multivariate analysis should be performed to determine if TME or DLS are independent predictors of benefit from chemotherapy.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added multivariate Cox regression analysis showing DLS is an independent predictor of chemotherapy benefit after adjusting for stage, age, and other clinical variables.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: For immunotherapy treatment — were patients treated with single agent or combination with chemo? If mixed, the analysis needs to be divided to study single agent and combination separately. It is unclear how heterogeneous this group is.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We clarified treatment regimens and performed subgroup analyses by treatment type.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The AUCs seem similar to their previous work (Jiang et al, Lancet Digital Health). Why AUC is used for measuring survival performance? Is the endpoint classification only at 5 years?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We clarified the survival endpoint definition and added time-dependent AUC analysis and C-index for survival prediction.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The choice of being more concerned with interpretability than explainability appears trenchant. If the authors have a strategy for dealing with explainability and determining criteria to select significant features, they should describe it.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We expanded the discussion to address both interpretability (biology-guided architecture) and explainability (feature attribution maps).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There is a general lack of details (data more than code) for the work to be reproduced.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We expanded methods section with full implementation details and made code available on GitHub.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: How many pathologists were involved in the TME classification? Was this done independently? How were conflicts resolved in TME assessments?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Two pathologists independently classified TME with a third resolving conflicts. Inter-rater agreement (kappa) reported.

reviewer_strengths.text: The results presented are valuable. The methodology is sound. The authors claim superior results compared to the literature.

entries.paper_title: Integration of pathologic characteristics, genetic risk and lifestyle exposure for colorectal cancer survival assessment
entries.prediction_task: Colorectal cancer 5-year survival prediction using polygenic prognostic score + clinical + lifestyle

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A significant methodological issue: the use of the same dataset for both GWAS and PPS parameterisation. This overlap will result in overfitting of PPS and optimism in performance estimates. This is clearly demonstrated by the drop in performance in the TCGA cohort where calibration and AUC are quite poor compared to the discovery cohorts.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We acknowledge this limitation and have added detailed discussion. We performed sensitivity analysis with stricter separation and noted the performance gap.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Reported statistics are limited to effect sizes (HR), AUC, and KM curves/log rank tests. Reporting of variance explained for the PPS would be helpful, in addition to clinically meaningful metrics such as sensitivity/specificity/PPV, and decision curve analysis.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We have added variance explained (R²), sensitivity/specificity at optimal thresholds, and DCA analysis.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Overwhelmingly the presence of stage and grade are the strongest predictors of survival (AUC 0.8 vs PRS alone 0.63). Whether the addition of PRS to a model containing stage and grade is of any value needs much more careful consideration than just reporting the increment in AUC.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added NRI analysis and DCA to demonstrate the incremental clinical value of PRS beyond stage/grade.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The combined model has been made publicly available for use 'in clinical practice'. This model has not been externally validated, having been constructed and tested only in the PLCO cohort, and I have very serious reservations about it being made available as such as a clinical tool.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We revised the language to state the tool is for research purposes only, not clinical practice. Added explicit disclaimer.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Handling of missing data noted in Table 1 and several supplementary tables is not reported — was complete case analysis used, or imputation in some form?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We clarified that multiple imputation was used for missing lifestyle variables and complete case analysis for genetic data.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the construction of the HLS — it is unclear why these particular predictors were chosen and how cut-off thresholds were defined. The 'traditional model' includes some but not all lifestyle predictors. Authors reference a pre-existing validated lifestyle model (Cheng et al) — is there a reason this was not used?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We justified predictor selection based on WHO guidelines and existing literature. Comparison with Cheng et al model added.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The paper does not report how cancer cases were identified in UKB (which field was used). End of follow-up/censoring dates should also be defined, as cancer data has been regularly updated.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added case identification methodology (ICD-10 codes from cancer registry) and specified censoring dates.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I would suggest that the number of cases does not constitute 'Large scale' GWAS meta-analysis. There is insufficient power to detect GWAS-significant SNP associations. This should be made clearer in the discussion.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We toned down the 'large scale' claim and added power analysis discussion.

reviewer_strengths.text: An interesting and innovative study that firstly introduces PPS (a germline variant score) into the colorectal cancer survival prediction. Multi-ancestry replication is a strength.

entries.paper_title: Development and validation of an interpretable model integrating multimodal information for improving ovarian cancer diagnosis
entries.prediction_task: Ovarian cancer diagnosis from ultrasound + clinical variables

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Identifying ovarian cancer in a woman with CA125 of 10,000 or massive ascites is not difficult. What would be of actual clinical value is an algorithm that is highly predictive in women with NORMAL CA125s, relatively small masses (<10 cm), without obvious clinical evidence of malignancy.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We showed that 44.6% had normal CA125 and 82.6% had lesions <10cm. OvcaFinder still achieved highest performance in these subgroups.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Nearly half of the training set of 724 masses were malignant, likely introducing significant bias limiting generalizability. In community settings, typically <5% of masses are malignant. Even in tertiary referral centers, usual prevalence is <25%.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We acknowledged the relatively higher malignancy rate in the limitation section. Both centers were high-level cancer hospitals in China. Added discussion of prevalence adjustment.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Inclusion of borderline tumors as malignant is problematic. Borderline tumors rarely cause death and surgery by gynecologic oncologist has no impact on survival. Show performance if only invasive cancers are included.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added sensitivity analysis excluding borderline tumors showing maintained performance for invasive cancers.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In assessing ORADS, sensitivity dropped from 96.2% (internal) to 85.7% (external). A difference between 96% and 86% is significant. An explanation as to why performance varied so much between external and internal datasets is needed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We analyzed sources of performance degradation and attributed differences to imaging equipment, operator expertise, and patient population differences between centers.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The unusual nature of the training set (nearly 50% malignant) and the lack of detail about how human input was provided makes it impossible to reproduce the work.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We expanded methods with full HITL protocol details, reader selection criteria, and scoring methodology.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors did not explain what DL specifically finds in ultrasound images. The explanation that it 'highlighted the most important areas' is laconic. Should explain what extent and localization of hotspots mean in benign vs malignant lesions.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added quantitative analysis of Grad-CAM hotspot patterns comparing benign vs malignant, including hotspot area percentage and spatial distribution.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Development of RF model serving as OvcaFinder lacks details. How were the sets of different predictors identified? Please expand the description.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We expanded the RF model development section with feature selection process and hyperparameter tuning details.

reviewer_strengths.text: The work is interesting in that there is significant interest in ML models for diagnostic imaging. No previously reported ML model used a similar strategy, so the report is novel.

entries.paper_title: Targeted plasma proteomics reveals organ damage signatures of AIDS- and noncommunicable disease-related deaths in people with HIV
entries.prediction_task: Mortality prediction in HIV patients using plasma proteomics panel

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Selection bias may be a concern as less than 6% of the original CHART cohort is included. How do baseline characteristics of selected patients compare to the overall population? Could patients have been matched with ART treatment in addition to age and sex?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added comparison of selected vs overall cohort characteristics and justified the sampling strategy. ART matching was not feasible due to heterogeneity.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Adjustments for the duration or type of ART use are conspicuously missing from the models. Several ART either act directly on viral or host proteins or indirectly through transcription. This could enhance models' accuracy.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added ART duration and type as covariates in sensitivity analyses. Results remained robust after adjustment.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Adjusting protein expression for renal function is important as several studies report the impact of renal function on protein expression due to the kidney's role in filtering and inflammatory response.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added eGFR as a covariate and performed sensitivity analysis stratified by renal function.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Throughout the study, the authors implied seeking unique proteomics signatures dichotomizing AIDS vs NCD deaths. However, figures compare each death type with HIV survivors separately. The conclusions could be totally different if all groups were compared against each other. A Venn diagram showing common proteins across all comparisons is needed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added comprehensive multi-group comparison analysis with Venn diagram and pairwise contrasts.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The paper fails to describe potential confounders. The time of plasma isolation and preservative type could introduce methodological artifacts. The time between plasma collection and death is not described. Authors state protein expression was altered 'right before' death but provide no time data.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We clarified sample collection protocols, added time-to-death analysis, and corrected temporal language.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The statistical approaches were not clear. Table 1 showed three P-values where ANOVA followed by post-hoc test should have been used. Tables include data not significant after FDR correction, making interpretation difficult.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We corrected statistical tests and removed non-significant results from main tables.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It is not clear why the validation cohort of 127 samples had significantly lower sensitivity than the training datasets. Supplemental Table 1 is missing.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We explained the performance gap due to smaller sample size and different clinical characteristics. Supplemental Table 1 added.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Several unsubstantiated statements imply causality throughout the results section. Introduction states 'traditional biomarkers are challenging for predicting mortality' but Discussion says they have 'potential for predicting mortality' — these are contradictory.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We revised causal language to associational framing and resolved the logical inconsistency between introduction and discussion.

reviewer_strengths.text: The report is appropriately written with appropriate statistical methods, prediction corrections, and a validation group. The markers identified (CA12, CA14) are consistent and potentially biologically relevant.

entries.paper_title: Real-time prediction of intensive care unit patient acuity and therapy requirements using state-space modelling
entries.prediction_task: ICU patient acuity and life-sustaining therapy prediction (4-hour horizon)

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The motivation for using Mamba is not clear. There doesn't seem to be a significant difference between APRICOT-T (Transformer) and APRICOT-M (Mamba). CatBoost and GRU appear competitive on many tasks while requiring far less computational resources.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added computational cost comparison and showed Mamba advantages in longer sequences and inference speed.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Confidence intervals computed using bootstrapping provide uncertainty related to the data sample but not related to model parameters. Also, using time-to-event analysis rather than binary classification could avoid issues related to time window choice.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We acknowledged this limitation and discussed model uncertainty vs data uncertainty. Time-to-event analysis added as supplementary comparison.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The abstract states the model 'was validated prospectively on data from 2021-2023' but Mamba was first introduced in 2023. It appears the model was 'retrospectively validated' on previously collected prospective data. Please clarify.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We clarified that the prospective data collection preceded model development, and the model was applied retrospectively to this prospectively collected dataset.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: One challenge with prediction of rare events is having low PPV. AUC tends to produce overly optimistic results. It would be insightful to repeat analysis in 50 patients from prospective cohort by at least three clinical adjudicators to determine clinical utility (were alerts timely, accurate, actionable?).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We added clinician review of alerts in a subset of prospective patients with assessment of timeliness and actionability.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Authors claim 'first SSM model application to clinical data' but there are multiple prior studies applying state-space models to clinical data (Yin 2021, Ghassemi 2017, Nemati 2013). Please explain how the proposed SSM differs from prior works.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We corrected the novelty claim to 'first Mamba-based SSM application' and added comparison with prior SSM clinical works.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Results for the temporal cohort were relegated to supplementary material. An extra column for the temporal cohort would not take up much space in the main article.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We moved temporal validation results to the main text.

reviewer_strengths.text: Major strength is that the model was validated on external, temporally shifted and prospectively collected data. Performed significantly better than the traditional SOFA score.
The curation and harmonization of such diverse datasets require tremendous efforts, and the authors should be applauded for their dedication.

entries.paper_title: Predicting in-hospital outcomes of patients with acute kidney injury
entries.prediction_task: In-hospital mortality and dialysis prediction in AKI patients (24h-7d)

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The use of a bidirectional RNN at any given point in time is using future data which would not be available for clinical decision. That is the point of a bidirectional RNN and the point of this criticism. Evaluation would be overly optimistic. This is a major flaw in the paper.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: We clarified that the bidirectional component operates within the historical data window only, not across the prediction boundary. Added unidirectional LSTM comparison.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The use of data from 20 past years is problematic — medicine has taken a great leap forward. Using a temporally remote population to predict future patients may not work. Instead of randomly splitting, temporal partitioning would more accurately estimate deployment performance.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The paper uses methodology that has been developed by others and is readily available for use in a convenient R package, 'personalized'; the contribution of this paper is the application of said methodology to personalization of cancer treatments. There is nothing wrong with that, but the author occasionally use language that obscures this important fact. For instance, the statements 'the study introduces an innovative approach' or 'this methodological framework aims to revolutionize treatment selection' in the abstract can be easily misunderstood.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acknowledged the comment, revised abstract language, and introduced an A-STEP ensemble framework as additional novel methodological contribution.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The CI methods are based on some important assumptions such as: no residual confounding, SUTVA, etc. These assumptions are not stated or discussed anywhere in the manuscript as far as I can tell, which would be important to do because they may not always be reasonable in practice.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added Supplementary Methods S2 explicitly stating no-residual-confounding, SUTVA, and treatment-ignorability assumptions and discussed their plausibility in practice.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The use of the word 'validation' in this study is problematic. The methodology hinges on estimating individual/group-specific treatment effects (ITE), which is only possible under strong assumptions. The 'validation' performed in this paper consists of estimating ITEs in a different dataset and then showing, essentially, that ITEs are higher for people who actually received the recommended treatment. However this doesn't 'validate' the model in the sense that the assumptions used to construct it are not checked. A more direct validation would need to use randomized data (could be retrospective), and would need to show that the actual treatment outcomes of patients who received the recommended treatments were better than those who did not.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added two external validation cohorts (Dana-Farber n=1077, Stand Up To Cancer n=393) and reported weighted risk-reduction (Table 3) plus Kaplan-Meier survival curves with hazard ratios, demonstrating better outcomes in patients who received model-recommended therapy.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: To the extent that validation was performed, there seems to be no check whether the 'treatment effects conditional on subgroups' are statistically significant. It seems like the 'personalized' package does provide methods to perform such tests. Additionally, correction for multiple testing could be needed given that 5 different loss functions were tried.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors performed FDR multiple-testing correction in revision; reviewer noted in Round 2 that only 1 of 8 tested models remained significant under correction, and questioned use of FDR 0.1 instead of Bonferroni.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: All five methods that were proposed in the original version of this manuscript failed to work in the two validation cohorts. I am afraid this was the reason why three new methods (H-STEP, S-STEP, and A-STEP) were also added, although that is not made clear. Of these three new methods, only A-STEP can be 'validated' in the two new cohorts; however, the p-values for the two arms are 0.016 and 0.0076. Since the authors have now tried 8 methods in total on this data, some kind of p-value correction should be applied to correct for this fact. So, in total, it could be questionable that the new proposed A-STAR method—which seems to have been developed using the validation data more than once—would actually generalize.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors performed FDR p-value correction but reviewer remained dissatisfied in subsequent round, noting that the corrected significance bar (FDR 0.1) is lenient and that the A-STEP method appears to have been developed using the validation set.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The methods are tested by determining the survival in the cohorts of those patients who receive the treatment recommended by the model to those who were not treated as recommended by the model. As remarked in the previous manuscript, direct validation of this kind of method would require analysis of a randomized rather than observational trial. While the authors do employ propensity score matching in an attempt to reduce confounding, we still need to buy that there is no residual confounding, which can be questionable since some important clinical variables seem to be missing (see comment by R4). Unfortunately, this point was not really addressed by the revision.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added discussion of residual confounding limitation but did not perform randomized validation; reviewer noted point remained inadequately addressed.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Their study hinges on their ability to identify and control for bias arising from intrinsic differences between patients selected for ICI-mono and ICI-chemo—the reviewer is not convinced that with their limited clinical data, that does not for example include Performance Status, they would be able to do this meaningfully. There is no description of how the genomic mutation markers were derived, or what they were, anywhere in the paper.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added clinical-variable list, expanded cohort to multiple centers, and clarified mutation feature derivation, but did not include Performance Status (likely unavailable in source data).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors choose to identify 3-months progression as a binary endpoint. I wonder why this choice was made rather than using the full survival data, since the R package 'personalized' supports time-to-event outcomes.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added progression-free-survival analyses (Kaplan-Meier with HRs) alongside binary 3-month endpoint in the revision.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors stated that they will only make the code available upon publication (p. 25) so I was unable to review the code.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors made code publicly available at https://github.com/WuLabMDA/A-STEP with documentation for replicating results.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: An issue for this reader with respect to the field of personalized medicine in general is the use of terminology, such as 'personalized immunotherapy' or the expression of an objective to seek 'optimal personalized treatment strategies' implying that the outcome of this work will be the identification of the optimal treatment for an individual. In fact, the process of determining the best treatment allocation can be viewed as a task of subgroup identification.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors softened language and clarified in Round 2 that the analysis is subgroup identification, and revised abstract/introduction tone in Round 3.

reviewer_strengths.text: A data driven and rigorous approach for this purpose. The use of multi-center data and the addition of external testing cohorts is notable.
I commend the authors for applying sound causal inference methodology in this field. These methods could be interesting for the development of personalized medicine.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The description of the study population is not sufficient. It is described that included individuals are those with T2D within 12 months prior to baseline, where baseline is the first recorded instance of T2D in the database. This makes no sense, as that would imply no T2D events prior to baseline.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that 'newly diagnosed T2D' (≤12 months) was the inclusion criterion using first-ever ICD-10 E11 record cross-checked against medical notes and prescriptions to confirm diagnosis date.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There is a lack of justification as to why individuals with major medical conditions were excluded (exclusion criteria (d)).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors justified exclusion of patients with malignancy, organ transplantation, ESRD to reduce confounding from intensive treatments and comorbidities; reviewer noted this also limits real-world applicability since ~33% of diabetes patients are multimorbid.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Outlier removal and rank normalization is performed without an explicit why (important!) and how (i.e. how was rank normalization in practice performed) and most importantly how many records it affects, and how it e.g. affects the results if it is not considered (as a sensitivity analysis). Adding complex data-preprocessing steps greatly increases model pipeline complexity so these choices should be justified.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors provided detailed justification (values >5 SD removed, n=575 outliers tabled by variable), explained that rank normalization ensures non-zero variance for DDRTree PCA step, and added sensitivity analysis to supplements.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There is a lack of detail in the description of the methods to a point where reproducing the experiments are impossible. The number of cross validation folds is not specified, and libraries of the machine learning algorithms considered are not specified, nor definitions of their hyperparameter spaces.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors expanded Methods section with details on 10-fold CV, hyperparameter search spaces, and library versions in revision.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It is claimed that the GBC method achieves 'highest accuracy' and therefore is chosen as a 'final model'. However, the authors are considering a multitude of outcomes so is that really the case for ALL of these? In addition, is accuracy really the best measure to consider? One could imagine that some of the considered outcomes are rare leading to class imbalance. Alternative measures not so sensible to class imbalance (e.g. ROC or PR AUC) should at the very least be considered for model selection, and at the very least reported. Further – there is no mention of how the prediction threshold was decided.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added ROC AUC and PR AUC for all models in revision; reviewer still flagged that hyperparameter selection process remained unclear.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Code availability: Given the lack of detail in the description of the methods and no code availability it is impossible to reproduce the presented results of the manuscript, even if one would have access to the data.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors expanded methods documentation; code availability not fully resolved in extracted pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It remains unclear whether the VAE is used for representation learning, feature selection, denoising, or all three, and why this choice is preferable to simpler alternatives (e.g. a vanilla autoencoder, PCA, or purely supervised selection). Assertions about 'informative' latent structure and 'denoised input' are not supported by comparative analyses.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified VAE role as feature ranking/selection and added LASSO/elastic-net comparison, but reviewer noted that implementation details (full-set vs subset, hyperparameter tuning, nested CV) remained ambiguous.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The manuscript lacks essential details on hyperparameter search spaces, selection criteria, and safeguards against data leakage. Model performance is reported without clear nested CV, fold definitions. It is also unclear when models use the full feature set versus the 10 'VAE-selected' features.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added clarifications but reviewer indicated several questions remained unanswered.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The proposed 'stability' metric based on cosine similarity across independently trained VAEs is not valid given rotational/permutation of latent spaces.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not fully resolved in extracted pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The inclusion of non-diabetic controls in representation learning is not sufficiently justified if the stated goal is to extract diabetes-specific patterns. reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors stated controls were included to enhance contrast for diabetes-specific phenotyping; reviewer remained unconvinced.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Statements about longitudinal 'phenotypic shift,' superiority of DDRTree over traditional clustering, mitigation of confounding via VAE-based selection, clinical relevance of the continuous model, and 'early interventions' are insufficiently supported by statistical testing, benchmarking, or appropriate references.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The observation was that HbA1c had modest effect, while lipids had the most substantial effect. The authors must consider reporting the burden of liver diseases in the sample for each diabetes complication explored in this manuscript as a table.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not fully described in extracted pages.

entries.paper_title: Graph augmented transformers improve chemotherapy toxicity symptom extraction from clinical notes

pdf_verification.note: PDF filename matches DOI shorthand s41467-026-72347-2

entries.prediction_task: Chemotherapy-toxicity symptom extraction from clinical notes via graph-augmented transformers

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The methods state that patients with 'blood cancers' were excluded, but the results note that hematopoietic tumors were the most prevalent cancer type and discuss lymphoma patients. The authors should clarify the hematologic malignancies permitted in the study.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that only leukemia patients were excluded per OP-35 specifications; lymphoma and multiple myeloma were retained. Methods updated to state this explicitly.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There is limited representation in the patient sample from certain patient races, and some cancer types are missing altogether (multiple myeloma, acute leukemia), which also can limit generalizability.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acknowledged limitation in discussion, emphasized need for future validation across more diverse populations and cancer types.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The manuscript also claimed this is a 'retrospective cohort study', which is a specific study method in traditional epidemiology. This is not accurate, the study is more like a methodology development.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors revised terminology to 'methodology development and a validation study using retrospective EHR data' throughout the manuscript.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It's not clear how the evaluation was done. Is it evaluated based on span match, exact match or flexible match? There is an inconsistency in evaluation metrics AUROC and F1 were used in various instances, why? Reporting of results need more details, for example, what's the percentage of … 'Specifically, they detected 7 patients with Pain, 1 with Anemia, 4 with symptoms 313 related to DVND, and 4 with diagnoses linked to NPFS.' What's the impact of the percentage?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that flexible match was used (model must detect at least one mention corresponding to annotated symptom), reported weighted AUROC, AUPRC, precision, recall, F1 at threshold 0.5, plus Hamming Loss and subset metrics for multi-label setting.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The experiments are insufficient and some details are missing. For example, it is unknown if GAT-CN has an advantage over other graph-based methods or even rule-based approaches. It would be interesting to see the results with the 'term nodes' concatenated as a sequence rather than form a graph as the input.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added Random Forest as rule-based-style baseline, included simple string-matching method using OP-35 Diagnosis Vocabulary, and argued that BioClinicalBERT (already in benchmark) serves as the sequence-based comparison; rule-based achieved 0.99 recall but 0.505 precision vs model's 0.780.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The current evaluation relies primarily on a single holdout test dataset. The absence of additional external or diverse datasets might limit insights into the generalizability of the GAT-CN model across various clinical settings or institutions.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acknowledged limitation in discussion, citing single-cancer-center single-holdout design, and committed to multi-institutional validation as future work.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Currently, the model's performance analysis is primarily reported using the F1 metric. Including additional sensitivity analyses, such as precision-recall curves, ROC curves, or decision threshold analyses, would offer deeper insights and further contextualize the model's performance, particularly regarding its sensitivity and specificity trade-offs.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added AUROC, AUPRC, precision, recall, F1 across symptom classes with PR and ROC curves.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: While the paper benchmarks the GAT-CN model against established transformer models, it should also include comparisons against newer state-of-the-art transformer models designed specifically for clinical text, such as Clinical-Longformer/BigBird and BioClinical ModernBERT.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors explained their reasoning in the revision; reviewer accepted in Round 2.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The supplementary materials lack detailed information regarding model training processes, specifically describing hyperparameter tuning procedures, parameter selection justifications, and including comprehensive training and evaluation loss curves. In the methods section, the manuscript does not describe the computational resources of deploying this model, including detailed metrics about training time, hardware requirements, resource utilization, and scalability.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added computational resource information to Methods section.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The discussion did not address subgroup performance disparities, particularly regarding ethnicity, offering detailed hypotheses for observed disparities and proposing concrete, actionable strategies to improve model fairness, such as diversifying training data, targeted fine-tuning, or fairness-aware algorithmic adjustments.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added limitation acknowledging subgroup disparities risk and need for hybrid approaches to mitigate bias.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the Results section, it is stated that the target cohort comprised 1753 patients who received acute care within 30 days of initiation of chemotherapy. However, in practical application for the proactive prediction of ACU events (as implied in the Introduction), the 30-day acute care status of patients would be necessarily unknown. If so, the applicability of the cohort to the intended task scenario might thus be further justified.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors revised terminology emphasizing the model performs symptom extraction temporally associated with toxicities rather than predictive ACU classification.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the Model Evaluation subsection, it is stated that the ground truth for model performance evaluation was generated by manual annotation on patients' clinical notes (obtained before t_1, from Figure 2). However, if the intended objective is proactive prediction, the relevant ACUs would arise only after the notes were recorded (i.e. after t_1, before t_f). If so, it might be clarified as to whether the annotation using the clinical notes (obtained before t_1) would reflect future patient ACU (after t_1).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors revised manuscript to clarify model identifies symptoms temporally associated with chemotherapy-induced toxicities rather than performing causal prediction of future ACU.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the Diagnosis Vocabulary and Note Annotation subsection, it is stated that the training and validation sets were labeled using patient OP-35 diagnosis codes in the EHR data, but the test set was manually annotated by four annotators. This difference in annotation between the training/validation and test sets might be explained - was annotation by diagnosis code inapplicable for the test set?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not fully extracted; authors revised methods.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the Model Evaluation subsection, benchmarking against existing transformer-based models and baseline approaches was described. An ablation experiment with different embeddings as input to the graph model might be appropriate, to support the chosen Bio+ClinicalBERT embedding. For the Random Forest baseline approach, it might be clarified as to whether hyperparameter optimization had been attempted.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not fully extracted; authors added rule-based baseline.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It is unclear how observer and internal technical variability regarding ultrasound (US) and contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) were addressed in the study. Please provide detailed information on how variability among different observers and technical settings was managed. This could include standardization procedures, training protocols for observers, inter-observer reliability assessments, and calibration methods used to ensure consistency across examinations.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors detailed expertise of radiologists (10-20+ years), guideline-based acquisition protocols, multi-vendor equipment specifications, subgroup analyses showing no significant variability across centers/manufacturers, and three ablation studies.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There is a discrepancy in the clinical settings between the development and validation sets, with the development set focusing on non-treated HCC and the validation set on recurrent HCC. Explain the rationale behind using different clinical settings for development and validation. Address how this difference might affect the model's performance and generalizability. Consider discussing any steps taken to mitigate potential biases introduced by this discrepancy.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors collected additional rHCC data from two hospitals for the external testing cohort and performed subgroup analyses showing consistent performance.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A cohort from center A was included as an external validation set, but the patients were treated, and the scans were performed at the same center as the development cohort, which challenges the definition of 'external validation.' To ensure proper generalization testing, consider including results from only truly external centers (e.g., centers B and C).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added subgroup analyses across Centers A through E showing consistent C-index (0.72-0.76) and AUC.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The paper fails to compare its results with state-of-the-art (SOTA) Vision Transformer-based models that support multimodal data or publicly available datasets. Vision Transformers rely on the quality and diversity of the dataset because their performance is tied to the patterns they learn during training. Without testing on different publicly available datasets, it is difficult to establish the generalizability and robustness of the proposed approach. Moreover, the diversity of the training data is important for training Vision Transformers. Any bias in the training data, such as race or gender bias, can affect the model's predictions.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors performed ablation studies including alternative DL models; SOTA ViT benchmarks on public datasets not added but multi-center Chinese cohorts emphasized.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Moreover, the comparisons with major guideline methods do not address inherent biases or limitations in the staging systems. This could undermine the validity of the results, as these biases can impact the model's performance. reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The study also does not provide detailed information on sex and gender considerations, failing to comply with the SAGER guidelines (as recommended in the review instructions).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added sex/age subgroup analyses in 2ndTA and 2ndSR datasets.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In addition, the statistical analysis lacks detailed justification for the selection of some specific tests and thresholds. reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not fully extracted in available pages; authors expanded methods.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The actual goal of your study and the algorithm is not making a decision regarding which local therapy to use or if it should be used at all but to give an outlook on the prognosis of the patient, namely the OS/PFS. Therefore the title is misleading. You do not investigate on how to improve HCC treatment. In order to give aid in the treatment decision, you would have to include patients in whom the therapy decision was wrong or suboptimal. But how do you know in your cohorts that the treatment they received was inferior to any other treatment option? You can't know that and neither your AI algorithm.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not extracted in available pages; reviewer recommended title change to 'prognostication tool in HCC to be treated by means of local therapy'.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: To include just T2w, DWI and CEUS sounds surprising. How did you decide to use these specific parts of the diagnostic work-up? What do you expect the AI to read on these images? We know that T2 signal and diffusion restriction loosely correlates with the grading of the tumors. What if you provided the algorithm with the grading of the tumors instead of MRI? Or to give just SI-values/radiomics from these images instead of letting the algorithm read this on its own? Or if you run the algorithm against sets of (para)clinical parameters, which are known to determine the prognosis and outcome of patients? reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not extracted in available pages.

pdf_verification.note: PDF filename matches DOI shorthand s41467-025-61887-8

entries.prediction_task: Clinical outcome prediction (Nature Comm 2025)

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Authors aimed to examine the potential of serum proteomics for improved risk stratification in ADPKD, as indicated in the abstract. However, data interpretation, as stated in the abstract, is not supported by results: authors cannot exclude that changes in serum proteome of ADPKD patients are the effect of eGFR decline per sé, in fact the study does not include a control group of patients with variable eGFR due to other causes.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added separate IgA nephropathy CKD control cohort (Figure S4, Table S10), included eGFR in multivariate models to control for collinearity, showed proteome markers retain independent predictive capacity, and added eGFR-dependency analyses within the ADPKD cohort (Table S9).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: eGFR slope calculation: Authors estimated annual eGFR slope. Please define the mean/median period of observation for the definition of mean annual eGFR decline.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added Table S1 detailing eGFR availability and timeframe (median follow-up 6.8/6.4/6.0 years; median 10/9/7 measurements; median intervals).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Identification of proteins associated with annual GFR slope: the authors indicate 4 serum proteins related to eGFR decline. In lines 187-88, authors comment 'highlighting their potential significance in the pathophysiology of renal function deterioration'. The study is not designed to show the causal relationship between serum changes and eGFR decline: the changes may represent the effect of eGFR decline.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors deleted pathophysiology wording and added limitations stating causality cannot be inferred; correlation analyses added.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Moreover, did the author correlate serum proteome to changes of renal volume? Besides eGFR decline, the increase in kidney volume is another parameter used in ADPKD clinical studies to address disease progression.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors explained serial TKV is not standard care per ERA Statement; longitudinal TKV unavailable in cohort. Cross-sectional TKV deemed limited added value.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Model Validation: The adjusted R² is reported at 0.31. It would be beneficial for the authors to compare this with other models beyond the Mayo Imaging Classification to contextualize whether an R² of 0.31 is considered robust.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors contextualized adjusted R² of 0.31 against literature, noted that TKV-based gold-standard models also show similar or lower R² values, and that adding genotype data improved performance further.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Patient Stratification: Considering that younger patients may not exhibit an eGFR slope >3 despite being at risk of rapid progression, it is advisable to stratify patients based on observed GFR rates (fast vs. slow) and predicted risks using both the Mayo Imaging Classification and PROPKD scores. It would be insightful to align proteomics biomarkers thresholds with these known progression rates.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added comparison using >3 ml/min/1.73m² cutoff (Figure S9: AUC 0.82 Combined Model, 0.69 MIC); explained thresholds for untargeted proteomics are not feasible due to relative quantification.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Clinical Application: A critical clinical question is the prediction of ESRD onset. The authors have predicted future eGFR but this information is relegated to a supplemental figure. Clarity on the accuracy and error of this prediction is needed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added RMSE accuracy metric, expanded figure 2D explanation, clarified ΔeGFR interpretation and provided detailed legend revision.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Proteomic Indicators: Is the mere presence of specific proteins indicative of a worse outcome? Establishing thresholds for these proteins, and correlating them with known biological activities in ADPKD, would enhance the utility of the findings. Furthermore, is it possible for each proteome to be predictive on its own?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors explained MS-based proteomics is relative quantification, not absolute; presented missingness analysis (FERMT3 19.4% missing; RARRES2 22.2% missing with negative eGFR-slope correlation); argued single proteins insufficient — multi-biomarker model required.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Impact of Therapy: In patients who received disease-modifying therapy, such as tolvaptan, were there any changes in the proteomics profile? This would be crucial for understanding the impact of such treatments on disease progression.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors checked subcohort of 20 patients on tolvaptan — no differentially regulated proteins detected (likely sample-size limited); flagged as future direction.

pdf_verification.note: PDF filename matches DOI shorthand s41467-025-61891-y

entries.prediction_task: Clinical outcome prediction (Nature Comm 2025)

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: UK Biobank has individuals who have kinship that is known to cause inflation for prediction models (Ellis 2024 AJHG). Since the model is fitting many predictors, there is a chance that the model is capturing subtle population structures that cross-validation could not remove. One solution is finding an external validation cohort; the other solution is making sure individuals in the training and testing don't have kinship (i.e. the same family are always in the training OR testing).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors restructured training/testing to use England+Wales for training and Scotland for testing as a proxy for external validation, and additionally excluded from the test set individuals sharing kinship (≥0.0442 coefficient, third-degree or closer) with any training-set member. Predictive performance remained stable under both stricter setups.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The c-index improvement is small and not easily interpretable (i.e. improvement from 0.6 to 0.7 has a very different interpretation than 0.7 to 0.8; even the same C-index with different incidence rate is not comparable). Is it possible to quantify the contribution of prediction power by the interaction terms (analogous to R2)? Previous study has shown that for traits with many small effects, non-additive variance is small.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added an incremental R² measure (ΔR²) based on Royston's R² for survival models and reported both incremental C-index and incremental R² in revised Figure 1, Table 1, and Supplementary Table 4.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Line 363 / Line 488 — what are the procedures for selecting hyperparameters? Line 494 mentioned grid search but did not specify what are the criteria used (is it based on cross validation of likelihood? Prediction C-index?).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Please provide more details on how prevalent cases were excluded. How did you exclude the prevalent diseases listed in ST2? Some of the diseases don't have primary care data available.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: How do the authors plan to visualize the KG and deliver to the users? Currently, the github is not available. The code is not available at the github site.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors made the GitHub repository public (https://github.com/MonsterTea/MDKG) with README and Python code execution instructions; Reviewer #3 confirmed availability in round 2.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: For the MDD study, how is the 2000 individual control chosen? Also, why choose MDD? This procedure seems to be standardized across other mental health disorders as well — to show robustness, maybe the authors could experiment on other diseases as well.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors addressed control selection and discussed generalizability of pipeline to other diseases.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Why is air pollution an important factor for MDD? Why do non-medical EHR embedding have such a good performance? Is there potential confounders? How do you select these variables to avoid confounders?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors addressed confounder selection rationale and feature provenance in revision.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Use of ChatGPT: While ChatGPT demonstrates impressive performance across many benchmarks, the choice of a closed, proprietary platform for constructing a shared knowledge graph is problematic. A key expectation for a knowledge graph project is that it should be built on an openly available large language model (LLM), rather than a closed system like OpenAI's platform. The use of closed systems hinders transparency in understanding the deeper structures of the knowledge graph, raising concerns about the potential for data misuse by third-party providers.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors retained ChatGPT/GPT-4o but added confidence scoring, contradiction handling, and human evaluation correlation (mean r=0.78). Reviewer #2 still found justification insufficient in round 2 but accepted the revision overall.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Reliability of Insights: There is a lack of clarity regarding how users can verify the reliability of insights derived from the knowledge graph, particularly those not covered by established medical databases. It is crucial when employing LLMs that users are encouraged to critically assess machine-generated content rather than blindly trust it. Hallucinations — a known issue in many domains involving LLMs — pose a specific risk. How has this been addressed or mitigated in the current implementation?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added a Confidence Score (combining prediction score, impact factor, frequency, distinct years, recency, contradiction penalty) detailed in Appendix C; manual evaluation showed mean correlation 0.78 with human-assigned scores.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Why have the authors focused on the use of PheCode over ICD-10? The authors include a line in the manuscript, however it needs more explanation. For an application of this research, would not prediction on ICD-10 codes be more meaningful?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors argued PheCodes avoid billing-practice confusion. Reviewer #2 in round 2 remained unconvinced and suggested simpler alternative (first two digits of ICD-10).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Clarification of 'Disease Prediction': The use of the term 'disease prediction' remains ambiguous. It is unclear if the authors are predicting future diagnoses or simply identifying patients already labeled with Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) in their dataset. The authors must explicitly clarify if their approach involves genuine predictive modeling — predicting future onset of disease — or merely labeling existing diagnoses accurately.

entries.prediction_task: Clinical outcome prediction (Nature Comm 2025)

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The model was trained by RNA-seq data of sandwich-cultured primary human hepatocytes with a short-term exposure (24 hours). The severe distortions of two-dimensionally cultured hepatocyte gene expression due to de-differentiation has been clearly reported. Moreover, a short time exposure might not be sufficient to mimic many idiosyncratic toxicities that typically occur only after multiple weeks to months. Will such a selection bias of training data cause biased mechanistic prediction of the DILI candidates? This should at least be discussed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Acknowledged 2D-culture limitations; added Suppl. Fig. S2 showing hepatocyte marker expression confirming identity at 24h; added discussion section noting that 'the exposure timepoint of 24 hours limit the detection of delayed or immune-mediated toxicities.'

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Why did the authors set the safety margin at 80? Is it an empirical value? Please specify the rationale of setting this value as cut-off since SMs of 30 are chosen in many other studies.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: MOS threshold of 80 selected by empirical optimization on held-out training data balancing sensitivity and specificity; clarified rationale in Results and Methods; threshold within literature range 10-100. Added Suppl. Fig. S5 panel B.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The numbers of drugs are not consistent and confusing across the manuscript and supplementary data files. While DILImap was claimed to include 300 drugs, the Results section mentions 177 DILI+ and 93 DILI- in the training set and 32 DILI+ and 14 DILI- in the validation data, which are 316 drugs. Supplementary Table shows a total of 299 drugs 'DILIMAP_RESULTS'.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified dataset counts and reconciled supplementary tables in revision.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the modeling process, it is unclear whether the cross-validation mode was done for using all drugs in DILImap or only the training data. No details on how the training and validation datasets were constructed/split were given. What approach was taken to minimize potential biases in the validation set? This information would be particularly important with the claimed 100% specificity.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Clarified that 5-fold stratified compound-level cross-validation was used (described as 'all samples from a single compound were held out together'). Reviewer #3 in round 2 acknowledged this as 'clear and appropriate for preventing data leakage' but asked for further wording polish.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Despite extensive comparisons with various assays, the study does not benchmark ToxPredictor against other computational models, such as DILIPredictor, DILIGeNN, etc., for the same drugs. No rationale or supporting data were presented when choosing random forest as the algorithm.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added benchmarking against state-of-the-art in silico models per response letter; clarified RF rationale in revision.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Why 30-fold cross-validation was chosen? This fold seems very high considering the small dataset of 300 drugs.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that 30-fold refers to ensembling (30 trained RF models), not stratified k-fold; subsequently revised wording to '30 models' / '30 ensemble members'.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Codes and data files were available through figshare and code ocean but not completely with many missing data files (e.g. DILImap_deseq2.h5ad). Please ensure all data files are provided.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Released full codebase via GitHub and PyPI, complete validation and processed training data, S3 bucket for reviewer access during peer review (with credentials provided in rebuttal).
